label: Arabi camel

names.text: Opened with WebFetch: the abstract and conclusions list Shanbali, Kenani, Maalia, Maganeen and Lahwee as Arabi-group camels; the discussion also places Kabbashi in the 'big Arabi' subtype, which is not added here. The source says Arabi is a group label for pack camels and that the Kenani is also known as the Rufaa camel; the Rufaa name is not added here because the source leaves open whether Arabi applies to it.

about.text: The Arabi is a Sudanese dromedary group classed as a dual-purpose camel for meat and milk. It is kept in Sinnar, Blue Nile, Gadaref and Kordofan states, and the source claims better milk performance than the Bushari, Anafi and other Sudanese types, though it gives no milk measurements.

sources.text: Opened with WebFetch. Dual purpose and the better-performance claim are from the abstract ('has better performance and higher milk production and considered as dual purpose camel (meat and milk)'). Locations: Kenani in Sinnar and Blue Nile states; Lahwee in Gadaref; Shanbali, Maalia and Maganeen in North Kordofan, with Shanbali and Maalia moving into South Kordofan. The milk claim rests on udder morphology ('well developed udders'), not on measured yield.

Opened with WebFetch. The country is from the source's study of Sudanese camels; the source does not describe where the Arabi group came from, so no origin place, regions beyond SD, or formation years are given.

Opened with WebFetch: 'considered as dual purpose camel (meat and milk)'; the discussion says they 'may be classified as dual purpose camels' and cites Wardeh (2004) for this. The authors call for further study of milk and meat performance.

gaps: Searched for and not found: milk yield per lactation and per year, lactation length, milk composition (the source has none); a breed-level population figure (the only figure, about 3.9 million camels for Sudan as a whole, is for all camels); a DAD-IS entry or risk status (searches surfaced none for the camel; the DAD-IS URL tried returned 404); origin and formation years. The source's own group membership is inconsistent (Kabbashi appears only in the discussion).
